contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Pay preprocessing cost only when the query volume, mutation model, memory budget, and preserved semantics make the total workload cheaper than repeated scans.

items.prompt: A static unsorted array will receive one million exact-membership queries. Reordering is allowed and all queries use the same comparison key. Which strategy is usually the stronger asymptotic choice?

options.text: Sort once, then binary-search each query.
Scan the full unsorted array for every query.
Binary-search the unsorted array without preprocessing.
Sort the array again before every query.

feedback.reason: Repeated queries can amortize a one-time ordering cost.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Let q be one million. Repeated scans cost q · O(n) = O(qn). Sorting the static data once costs O(n log n), then q exact binary searches cost O(q log n), for O(n log n + q log n) total. The same ordered representation is reused, so the sort is not paid per query.
Contrast the strategies

This comparison is legal only because every query uses the sort key and reordering preserves the output contract. Binary-searching unsorted data has no discard proof, while sorting before every query destroys reuse and costs O(qn log n).

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: For static repeated queries, compare `one build + q lookups` with `q direct scans`.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_each: This repeats O(n) work one million times.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_unsorted: In unsorted data, a midpoint comparison cannot prove that either half lacks the target.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_each_query: Re-sorting unchanged data before every query repeats O(n log n) setup that one retained order avoids.

items.prompt: The same unsorted array will receive only one exact query. Which default asymptotic strategy is preferable when no sorted representation already exists?

options.text: Scan once in O(n).
Sort in O(n log n) and then binary-search.
Binary-search directly.
Build a sorted copy and discard it immediately after the query.

feedback.reason: The query count changes whether preprocessing can pay for itself.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

One scan inspects at most n elements, so it costs O(n). Building an ordered representation for this single query costs O(n log n) to sort before the O(log n) lookup, and its setup cannot be reused afterward.
Contrast the strategies

Binary search on the original array is incorrect because no midpoint comparison can discard a half. A sorted copy would preserve the original but add O(n) space and the same unnecessary sorting cost, so scanning is the stronger default under this workload.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Preprocessing is an investment; with no later reuse, include its full cost in the one query.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_then_binary: For one query, preprocessing dominates the logarithmic lookup.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_unsorted: The method is incorrect on arbitrary unsorted data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.build_and_discard: Building a disposable copy adds sorting time and linear space without any later query to reuse them.

items.prompt: A sorted copy is built for repeated key lookups, but the output must return the earliest original position for each key. What must the preprocessing preserve?

options.text: Each indexed key must retain enough original-position provenance to answer the earliest-position contract.
Only the sorted key value.
Only the number of records.
The midpoints used during queries.

feedback.reason: Preprocessing is legal only when the indexed representation can answer the complete output contract.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Sorting by key groups equal records but does not, by itself, encode which equal record appeared earliest in the original input. Store each record's original position and order or aggregate duplicates so the lookup can return the minimum position required by the contract.
Contrast the strategies

A key-only binary search can prove that the key exists but cannot recover the required identity. If the index omits provenance, scanning the original remains correct; midpoint history and array length contain no mapping from a key to its earliest source position.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Preserve every field needed to reconstruct the promised result, not only the field used to locate it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.key_only: Equal keys can map to different source positions, so the key alone cannot identify the earliest one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.array_length: The record count contains no mapping from an equal key to its earliest source position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_history: Visited midpoint positions describe the search process, not the matched record's original insertion position.

items.prompt: The dataset changes after almost every query. A sorted copy would need to be rebuilt from scratch after each update. Which factor moves the decision boundary back toward scanning?

options.text: The repeated preprocessing or maintenance cost can exceed the saved query work.
The word sorted still makes binary search mandatory.
Queries return booleans.
Midpoint arithmetic remains O(1).

feedback.reason: A preprocessing strategy must include update frequency and index maintenance.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The static model pays O(n log n) once. If almost every query follows an update that forces a full rebuild, the workload instead pays that setup repeatedly—potentially O(qn log n)—which can exceed O(qn) direct scanning.
Contrast the strategies

The boolean result and O(1) midpoint arithmetic do not remove rebuild work. The decision can still favor a different incrementally maintained index, but its update cost and freshness contract must be included rather than assuming sort-once reuse.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Evaluate one update-and-query epoch, then multiply it; a large lifetime query count can hide repeated setup.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_keyword: A stale or repeatedly rebuilt representation changes the total workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_boolean: A boolean output removes result materialization but does not make a stale index correct or cheap to rebuild.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_constant: The dominant cost may be rebuilding the representation.

items.prompt: A stable sorted random-access array receives repeated exact queries. No preprocessing is needed. Which comparison is appropriate?

options.text: Use correct binary search for O(log n) per query rather than O(n) scan per query.
Scan because preprocessing cost is zero for both.
Sort before every query to guarantee order.
Use any function called binarySearch without checking its boundaries.

feedback.reason: When the legal ordered representation already exists, repeated queries expose the direct O(log n) versus O(n) contrast.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The existing sorted random-access representation already supplies the binary-search invariant and O(1) midpoint access. Each aligned exact query therefore costs O(log n), while a scan can inspect O(n) values; over q queries the totals are O(q log n) and O(qn).
Contrast the strategies

No setup term needs amortizing here, and sorting again adds work without changing the invariant. The implementation must still maintain correct boundaries and compare the same key that defines the order; the function name alone proves neither.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Existing order removes preprocessing cost, but not the need to verify key alignment, random access, and boundary correctness.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_because_no_setup: The existing order already supplies the binary-search invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_again: Re-sorting an unchanged ordered array adds O(n log n) work without improving query legality.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_by_name_only: A function name does not guarantee correct interval boundaries, termination, or comparison with the actual sort key.

items.prompt: A sorted linked list receives many exact queries. What preprocessing can change the cost boundary most directly?

options.text: Materialize a stable random-access array once, then binary-search it for later queries.
Repeatedly locate linked-list midpoints by traversal and call that O(log n).
Rename nodes to left, right, and mid.
Scan and sort the linked list for every query.

feedback.reason: Preprocessing can change the data-access model as well as its order.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The linked list is sorted but lacks O(1) midpoint access, so locating successive midpoints by traversal does not deliver an O(log n) time lookup. Copying its n values once into a stable array costs O(n) time and O(n) space, after which each of q queries costs O(log n).
Contrast the strategies

The resulting O(n + q log n) total can beat q O(n) list scans when q is large enough and the list stays unchanged. Renaming nodes does not change access cost, and rebuilding or sorting per query throws away the reuse that justifies materialization.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Order permits discard; random access determines whether reaching each midpoint is actually cheap.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reuse_linked_mid: Walking a linked list to each midpoint adds traversal work that the O(log n) comparison count omits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rename_nodes: Renaming node references cannot provide constant-time access to an arbitrary midpoint position.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_and_sort_each: Sorting or rematerializing before every lookup eliminates the reuse that makes preprocessing worthwhile.

items.prompt: Memory is tightly limited and a sorted copy would require O(n) additional storage. The original unsorted data receives a moderate number of queries. What should the decision include?

options.text: Compare repeated scan time with both preprocessing time and the O(n) memory requirement; binary search is not automatically preferable.
Choose binary search because space never affects strategy selection.
Sort the original in place even if original order is part of the contract.
Treat every scan as O(1) because no extra memory is used.

feedback.reason: Repeated-query optimization is constrained by legal mutation and memory budget.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

A separate sorted copy costs O(n) extra space in addition to its build time. Sorting the original in place avoids that copy only if mutation and loss of original order are permitted; the prompt explicitly leaves those constraints open.
Contrast the strategies

With a tight memory budget or an original-order output contract, repeated O(n) scans can be the only legal representation even when they are slower. The choice must compare time, space, mutation rights, provenance, and the actual moderate q rather than applying an asymptotic slogan.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: An asymptotically faster lookup is unusable when its representation violates space or output constraints.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_memory: The sorted copy may violate the memory constraint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_in_place_always: In-place sorting can destroy original-order semantics or violate an immutability contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_constant_time: Using O(1) extra space does not change a scan's O(n) element inspections into constant time.

items.prompt: A preprocessed sorted index supports fast lookups, but queries sometimes use a different field than the indexed sort key. Which strategy applies to those unmatched queries?

options.text: Scan for that field or build and maintain another query-aligned index if workload justifies it.
Binary-search the existing index because any sorted order is sufficient.
Check the other field only at mid and discard a side.
Return a record matching the indexed field instead.

feedback.reason: Preprocessing is query-specific.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

An index sorted by field A makes comparisons on A monotonic across its positions. A predicate on unrelated field B can be true, false, then true again in that same order, so testing B at a midpoint cannot exclude either half.
Contrast the strategies

Scan the records for B, or build a B-aligned index if enough B queries repay its build and maintenance. Reusing the A index or returning an A match would either be unjustified or change the requested query.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: An ordered index accelerates only the predicates and outputs that its key and metadata encode.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reuse_any_index: The query predicate is not monotonic in the unrelated key order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_mid_field: A midpoint value of the unrelated field implies nothing about that field on either side.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_key_match: Returning a match on the indexed field answers a different question from the caller's predicate.

items.prompt: Which factors determine whether sorting once and binary-searching repeated queries is worthwhile? Select all that apply.

options.text: The number of queries q.
How often updates invalidate or require maintaining the sorted representation.
Whether reordering or the index preserves the full output contract.
Whether the query helper is called search.

feedback.reason: Preprocessing decisions are workload and contract decisions.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Query count q determines how often a per-query saving is reused. Mutation rate determines whether order remains valid or incurs maintenance. Semantic legality determines whether the reordered or indexed representation can still return the required identity and output.
Contrast the strategies

These three factors jointly decide the strategy: first reject representations that cannot answer correctly, then compare build plus maintenance plus queries over one lifetime. A helper's name contributes neither a cost term nor a correctness guarantee.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A preprocessing decision needs a legal representation and a workload that repays it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.function_name: A function name does not prove query alignment, index freshness, or any operation cost.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.query_count: Each additional query repeats scan work but reuses one valid ordered representation, shifting the total-cost comparison.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.mutation_rate: Updates can invalidate order or add repair and rebuild costs that erase lookup savings.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.semantic_legality: An index that loses required provenance or changes output semantics cannot replace a correct scan regardless of speed.

items.prompt: Which costs belong in the total workload for a sorted-copy binary-search strategy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Copying the original data when mutation is not allowed.
Sorting or otherwise constructing the ordered index.
The sum of all q binary-search query costs.
No cost for updates that rebuild the index.

feedback.reason: The total cost is preprocessing plus queries plus any maintenance.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

When the original cannot be mutated, creating the separate representation incurs copy time and O(n) storage. Ordering or indexing that representation incurs construction cost. Every one of q lookups contributes its query cost, and later updates contribute repair or rebuild work.
Contrast the strategies

The complete model is `copy + build + maintenance + q × query + output`. Omitting any paid term makes the indexed strategy appear cheaper than the system actually experiences; treating updates as free is especially wrong when they invalidate the representation.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Compare strategies over the same lifecycle and include every term they move between setup, update, query, and output.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_updates: An update that repairs or rebuilds the index consumes real work and is required for correct fresh queries.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.copy_cost: When mutation is forbidden, constructing a separate index requires copying or materializing the source records.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sort_cost: The sort or index build creates the ordered structure that makes half-discard legal.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.query_costs: The total includes all q lookups, not the cost of one representative binary search.

items.prompt: Which workloads favor repeated linear scans? Select all that apply.

options.text: Very few queries on unsorted data with no existing index.
Updates force a full index rebuild before most queries.
The output contract depends on original order and no provenance-preserving index is available.
Many aligned queries on a stable sorted random-access array.

feedback.reason: Scanning can win through lower setup cost, lower memory, or stronger semantic fit.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Few queries may not repay index construction. Rebuilding before most queries repeats setup so often that direct scans can cost less. If original-order identity is required and no provenance-preserving index exists, scanning is the correct representation regardless of speed.
Contrast the strategies

Many aligned queries on a stable sorted random-access array are the opposite case: the legal representation already exists and is reusable, so O(log n) lookups avoid repeated O(n) scans. Scanning is not inherently primitive; it wins when setup, maintenance, memory, or semantics cross the boundary.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Prefer the lowest complete legal workload cost, even when that means repeating a simple scan.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stable_many_sorted: Stable aligned order and many reusable queries favor O(log n) binary lookup rather than repeated scans.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.few_queries: With little reuse, one O(n log n) build can cost more than the few O(n) scans it replaces.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.frequent_rebuild: Paying full setup before most queries can erase the per-query saving from binary lookup.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.illegal_reorder: Without provenance-preserving structure, a reordered index cannot return the original-order identity that the contract requires.

items.prompt: Which changes can move a workload from scan-preferred to binary-search-preferred? Select all that apply.

options.text: Increase the number of aligned queries while keeping data stable.
Receive the data already sorted in random-access form.
Maintain an index incrementally at acceptable update cost.
Change the query to an arbitrary nonmonotonic condition.

feedback.reason: The decision boundary responds to query volume, representation, and maintenance.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Increasing aligned query count spreads one setup cost over more lookups. Receiving query-aligned sorted random-access data removes that setup term. An incrementally maintained index can preserve legal order without a full rebuild when its update cost fits the workload.
Contrast the strategies

Each accepted change improves reuse or representation while preserving correctness. An arbitrary nonmonotonic predicate removes the half-discard rule instead, so more queries cannot make binary search legal on that predicate.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A scan-to-binary transfer needs either reusable legal order or a workload that can afford to create and maintain it.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.arbitrary_predicate: A nonmonotonic truth pattern removes the implication needed to discard one side after a midpoint check.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.increase_q: More aligned queries reuse the same index and increase the repeated-scan work that preprocessing can replace.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.existing_sorted: Existing query-aligned random-access order removes build cost and immediately supports legal O(log n) lookup.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.maintained_index: Affordable incremental maintenance keeps the ordered structure fresh so later queries retain legal fast access.

items.prompt: Arrange the analysis of repeated-query preprocessing.

elements.text: State n, query count q, update frequency, and required outputs.
Describe repeated scan and each legal preprocessed representation.
Derive preprocessing, maintenance, per-query, memory, and output costs.
Choose the strategy for the actual workload and identify when the choice would flip.

feedback.reason: Repeated-query decisions require a complete workload model.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

items: State n, q, update frequency, output identity, mutation rights, and memory limits for one representation lifetime.
List repeated scanning and only the preprocessed representations that can answer the full contract.
For each, derive build, maintenance, all-query, output, and space costs.
Choose from the complete totals and state the workload or constraint change that would reverse the choice.

blocks.text: Contrast the strategies

Workload and contract come first because they decide which representations are legal and how often costs repeat. Totals come after candidate representations because construction and update terms depend on the design. The flip condition confirms that the break-even boundary, not a preferred algorithm name, drove the choice.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Model one full lifecycle—setup, updates, all queries, outputs, and space—before comparing strategies.

items.prompt: Arrange the lifecycle of a sorted-copy strategy for stable data.

elements.text: Copy the data if original order or immutability must be preserved.
Retain the representation for future queries instead of rebuilding it.

feedback.reason: The representation must exist and persist before repeated queries can amortize it.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

items: Copy the records once when original order or immutability prevents in-place mutation.
Sort the query representation once by the key used by every supported lookup.
Keep that representation alive and fresh so its construction can be reused.
Run each aligned query with binary search against the retained representation.

blocks.text: Contrast the strategies

Retention belongs before the repeated-query phase as a lifecycle commitment: if the representation is discarded or rebuilt for each query, the intended O(n log n + q log n) model becomes repeated setup. If updates occur, freshness maintenance must be inserted before affected queries.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Amortization requires one valid representation to survive across the queries that repay its construction.

items.prompt: Arrange the review after an update to preprocessed search data.

elements.text: Determine whether the update preserves the index ordering and metadata.
Apply the required incremental repair or full rebuild.
Verify queries will not read stale structure.
Use binary search only after the ordered representation is valid again.

feedback.reason: A stale index invalidates correctness, not just performance.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

items: Classify what the update changed: key order, indexed membership, provenance metadata, or none of them.
Apply the smallest correct repair, or rebuild when incremental repair cannot restore the invariant.
Verify the representation reflects the committed source state and preserves required output metadata.
Resume binary lookup only after midpoint discard and returned identities are valid again.

blocks.text: Contrast the strategies

Classification precedes repair so the system does not rebuild unnecessarily or miss affected metadata. Freshness verification precedes lookup because a stale but sorted index can return a plausible wrong answer. Every repair or rebuild contributes to the indexed strategy's total cost.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Never trade freshness for speed: binary search is legal only on the current ordered representation.

items.prompt: An unsorted static array of n values receives q exact queries. Compare q linear scans with sorting once and then binary-searching all queries.
constraints: Comparison sorting costs O(n log n).
Each binary search costs O(log n).

preprocessed_time: O(n log n + q log n)
O(n log n + q log n)

preprocessed_time.sort_plus_queries: O(n log n + q log n)

feedback.reason: The workload comparison includes both setup and every query.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Each scan can inspect n values, so q scans cost q · O(n) = O(qn). Sorting the static array once costs O(n log n), and q binary searches cost q · O(log n), giving O(n log n + q log n). Static data is the condition that lets the sort term appear once.
Contrast the strategies

For small q, the setup term can exceed the avoided scans; as q grows, the query savings can repay it. This formula compares time only after confirming that sorting or copying is legal and that every query aligns with the order.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Write the full totals: direct work is `q × n`; indexed work is `n log n + q log n`.

items.prompt: Using the same model, approximately which symbolic query scale makes sorting once competitive with repeated scans for large n?
constraints: Compare qn with n log n + q log n.
Treat n - log n as Θ(n) for large n.

feedback.reason: The setup cost becomes amortized after roughly logarithmically many full-array scans.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Set the dominant totals equal: qn ≈ n log n + q log n. Rearranging gives q(n − log n) ≈ n log n, so q ≈ n log n / (n − log n). For large n, n − log n = Θ(n), which reduces the crossover to q = Θ(log n).
Contrast the strategies

This is a symbolic boundary, not a deployment threshold: comparison constants, cache behavior, copying, memory, and query distribution can move the measured crossover. The derivation explains why Θ(1) queries generally do not amortize comparison sorting, while logarithmically many can.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Derive break-even by equating complete workloads; do not guess it from the per-query classes.

items.prompt: A sorted copy of n records is built and stores each record plus its original index. q binary searches are then performed. Select total time and additional representation space.

time: O(n log n + q log n)
O(n log n + q log n)

time.copy_sort_queries: O(n log n + q log n)

feedback.reason: Preserving original identity can make preprocessing correct but consumes linear extra memory.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Copying n records and their original indices consumes Θ(n) additional representation space. Sorting that copy costs O(n log n), and q binary searches add O(q log n), so total time is O(n log n + q log n); the initial O(n) copy is dominated by sorting.
Contrast the strategies

The stored original index makes the output contract recoverable but does not come for free. If the O(n) memory budget is unavailable, a slower scan of the source can remain the legal strategy even when the time formula favors preprocessing.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Provenance repairs result semantics by adding one stored source position per indexed record, hence Θ(n) extra space.

items.prompt: A dataset receives u updates. After each update, a full O(n log n) sorted index rebuild occurs, followed by r binary-search queries. Compare this with scanning each of the ur queries without an index.
constraints: n is treated as the same scale for each update epoch.

rebuild_strategy_time: O(u n log n + u r log n)
O(n log n + r log n)
O(u n log n + u r log n)

rebuild_strategy_time.per_epoch_rebuild_and_queries: O(u n log n + u r log n)

feedback.reason: Update frequency creates a new break-even comparison per epoch.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

There are u update epochs. Each rebuild costs O(n log n), contributing O(u n log n); each epoch then performs r binary searches, contributing O(u r log n). The rebuild strategy totals O(u n log n + u r log n). Scanning r times in every epoch costs u · r · O(n) = O(ur n).
Contrast the strategies

The relevant reuse count is r between rebuilds, not only total q = ur. A large lifetime query count can still lose if each epoch is too short to repay O(n log n); compare the two formulas under the actual u:r ratio or evaluate an incrementally maintained structure.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Partition dynamic workloads into freshness epochs and charge setup to each epoch that invalidates the index.

items.prompt: A sorted linked list is copied once into an array in O(n), then q exact queries use O(log n) binary search. Compare with q linked-list scans.
constraints: The copied array uses O(n) additional space.

feedback.reason: Preprocessing can create random access as well as preserve order.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Traversing the sorted list once and writing n values to an array costs O(n) time and O(n) additional space. The array then supports q binary searches at O(log n) each, so its total is O(n + q log n). Repeating a linked-list scan q times costs O(qn).
Contrast the strategies

No O(n log n) sort appears because the source list is already ordered; preprocessing changes access, not order. The array wins only when it remains fresh for enough queries and the O(n) extra memory fits.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Materialization cost is `one traversal + stored copy`; its payoff is constant-time midpoint access for every later search.

items.prompt: Each key comparison costs C. A stable sorted array receives q exact queries. Compare q binary searches with q linear scans.
constraints: Binary search performs O(log n) comparisons per query.
A scan performs O(n) comparisons per query in the worst case.

feedback.reason: Expensive comparisons multiply both strategies, while binary search reduces how many comparisons are needed.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

One binary search performs O(log n) key comparisons, each costing C, so q searches cost O(qC log n). One scan performs O(n) comparisons, so q scans cost O(qnC). C multiplies both counts; binary search wins by reducing the number of comparisons when its invariant is legal.
Contrast the strategies

Expensive comparisons can magnify the practical difference, but they do not establish sorted alignment, random access, or correct boundaries. Those correctness assumptions must be proved before applying either count.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Compute `number of comparisons × cost per comparison`; do not drop C from only one strategy.

items.prompt: A maintained ordered index supports O(log n) query and O(n) update. A plain array supports O(n) query and O(1) append. For q queries and u appends, compare total workload time.
constraints: The O(n) index update includes maintaining sorted order.

feedback.reason: The best representation depends jointly on query and update volume.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The indexed model performs q queries at O(log n) and u updates at O(n), totaling O(q log n + un). The plain array performs q scans at O(n) and u appends at O(1), totaling O(qn + u). Each formula includes both operation types.
Contrast the strategies

High q favors the indexed query term, while high u can make its linear update term dominate. Compare the totals for the actual mix; an ordered structure with a different update bound would be a different candidate and needs its own formula.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A representation moves cost between operations, so optimize for the complete q:u workload rather than lookup alone.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Pay preprocessing cost only when the query volume, mutation model, memory budget, and preserved semantics make the total workload cheaper than repeated scans.
